walkthroughs.title: Foundations: training finds the rule
walkthroughs.blurb: Fit a line to miles-to-km examples and watch the errors shrink to zero.

steps.title: Programming versus learning
steps.text: In traditional programming a person writes the rules and the computer turns data into answers. In machine learning you supply data and the answers, and the computer works out the rules. The rules it finds are called the model.

steps.title: Examples with known answers
steps.text: Three (miles, km) pairs. Nobody tells the computer how to convert them. The model will be a line y = m*x + b, and m and b are the parameters training must find.

steps.title: Start with a guess: m = 1, b = 0
steps.text: Predicted km = 1 * miles + 0. Error = actual - predicted. The errors are 3, 6 and 12: a poor model.

steps.title: Adjust the parameter: m = 1.5
steps.text: Predicted km = 1.5 * miles. The errors shrink to 0.5, 1 and 2. Training repeats this: change the parameters, check the errors, keep changes that help.

steps.title: Adjust again: m = 1.6
steps.text: Every prediction now matches, so the errors are 0. Training has found the parameters m = 1.6 and b = 0. That line is the model.

steps.title: Use the model on a new value
steps.text: A distance the model never saw: 50 miles. Predicted km = 1.6 * 50 + 0 = 80. Miles and km rise together in a straight line, a correlation near +1.

walkthroughs.title: kNN: classify a new point by voting
walkthroughs.blurb: Measure, sort, take the k nearest, vote, then see how k changes the answer.

steps.title: Start: a new point to classify
steps.text: Five labelled points, each Red or Blue, are known. A new, unlabelled point sits at (5, 5). kNN labels it by looking at its nearest neighbours.

steps.title: Measure the distance to each known point
steps.text: Straight-line (Euclidean) distance = square root of (across^2 + up^2). For a (8, 9): across 3, up 4, so sqrt(9 + 16) = 5.

steps.title: Sort by distance, nearest first
steps.text: kNN has no training step beyond remembering the points. The work happens now, at prediction time.

steps.title: Take the k = 3 nearest
steps.text: With k = 3 the neighbours are c (Red), b (Blue) and a (Blue).

steps.title: Majority vote
steps.text: Blue 2, Red 1, so the new point is classified Blue. An odd k means a two-class vote cannot tie.

steps.title: Change k and the answer can change
steps.text: k = 1 uses only c, so Red. k = 3 gives Blue. k = 5 uses all five points: Red 3, Blue 2, so Red. A small k follows noise; a large k blurs the boundary. k is a hyperparameter, chosen by you, not learned.

walkthroughs.title: k-fold cross-validation
walkthroughs.blurb: Five rounds, each fold takes a turn as the test set.

steps.title: Cut the data into k = 5 folds
steps.text: 100 rows split into 5 folds of 100 / 5 = 20 rows each. Every row sits in exactly one fold.

steps.title: Round 1: fold 1 is the test fold
steps.text: Fold 1 (20 rows) is held out for testing. Train on the other 4 folds (80 rows). The model's score on it is 0.82.

steps.title: Round 2: fold 2 is the test fold
steps.text: Fold 2 (20 rows) is held out for testing. The model's score on it is 0.78.

steps.title: Round 3: fold 3 is the test fold
steps.text: Fold 3 (20 rows) is held out for testing. The model's score on it is 0.85.

steps.title: Round 4: fold 4 is the test fold
steps.text: Fold 4 (20 rows) is held out for testing. The model's score on it is 0.80.

steps.title: Round 5: fold 5 is the test fold
steps.text: Fold 5 (20 rows) is held out for testing. The model's score on it is 0.80.

steps.title: Average the five scores
steps.text: (0.82 + 0.78 + 0.85 + 0.80 + 0.80) / 5 = 4.05 / 5 = 0.81. Every row was used for testing exactly once and for training k - 1 = 4 times, so the estimate depends less on one lucky or unlucky split.

walkthroughs.title: k-means clustering, one round at a time
walkthroughs.blurb: Assign points, move centroids, repeat until nothing changes.

steps.title: Start: two centroids
steps.text: Cluster six numbers into k = 2 groups. Pick two starting centroids at random from the data: c1 = 1 and c2 = 4. k-means is unsupervised: there are no labels.

steps.title: Assign every point to its nearest centroid
steps.text: Measure each point to both centroids (c1 = 1, c2 = 4) and join the closer one. The point 4 is distance 0 from c2, so it joins B. The point 2 is 1 from c1 and 2 from c2, so it joins A.

steps.title: Move each centroid to the mean of its cluster
steps.text: A = {1, 2} has mean 1.5. B = {4, 10, 11, 13} has mean 38 / 4 = 9.5. The centroids move: c1 = 1.5, c2 = 9.5.

steps.title: Assign again, using the moved centroids
steps.text: With c1 = 1.5 and c2 = 9.5 the point 4 is 2.5 from c1 but 5.5 from c2, so it switches from B to A. Assignments can change when the centroids move.

steps.title: Assign once more: nothing changes, so stop
steps.text: Every point picks the same cluster as before, so moving the centroids again would give the same result. The algorithm has converged. Different starting centroids can end in different clusters, which is why k-means is often run several times.

walkthroughs.title: The machine learning workflow, stage by stage
walkthroughs.blurb: Nine stages from loading data to monitoring the live model.

steps.title: 1. Load
steps.text: Read the dataset into the program, for example a CSV file into a pandas table.

steps.title: 2. Explore
steps.text: Look at it with pandas and charts: its size, the columns, odd values, how the columns relate.

steps.title: 3. Transform
steps.text: scikit-learn needs numbers, so text columns are converted (encoding) and scales are aligned.

steps.title: 4. Split
steps.text: Hold some rows back as a test set: x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(x, y, test_size=0.2). With 150 rows that is 120 to train on and 30 to test.

steps.title: 5. Create
steps.text: Pick an algorithm and make the model object. Nothing is learned yet.

steps.title: 6. Train + test
steps.text: model.fit(x_train, y_train) learns from the training rows; then model.predict(x_test) is compared with y_test.

steps.title: 7. Tune
steps.text: Adjust the hyperparameters, re-test, and check the accuracy. Only the model is changed, not the test rows.

steps.title: 8. Predict
steps.text: Use the model on live data it has never seen. This is what it was built for.

steps.title: 9. Monitor
steps.text: Watch the live model. If its results drift, tune, retrain or redeploy.

walkthroughs.title: Feature selection with RFE
walkthroughs.blurb: Train, drop the weakest feature, repeat, and see how the families compare.

steps.title: Start: four inputs to predict a house price
steps.text: RFE (recursive feature elimination) is a wrapper method: it builds a model, drops the weakest feature, and repeats. Goal here: keep the best 2 of 4 features.

steps.title: Round 1: train a model on all four
steps.text: The model scores how much each feature helps (illustrative numbers). street_number scores lowest.

steps.title: Drop the weakest: street_number
steps.text: It is eliminated first, so it is ranked last (4th).

steps.title: Round 2: train again on the remaining three
steps.text: A new model is built without street_number, and the scores are recalculated. age is now the weakest.

steps.title: Drop the weakest: age
steps.text: age is eliminated second, so it is ranked 3rd.

steps.title: Stop at two features
steps.text: area and rooms are what is left, so they are the selected features. Features are ranked by the order they were eliminated; the survivors rank best.

steps.title: How RFE compares with the other families
steps.text: RFE trains many models, so it is slow but very effective. A filter only scores each feature by itself, with no model, so it is fast but less effective. LASSO is embedded: selection happens while one model is fitted.

walkthroughs.title: PCA versus LDA
walkthroughs.blurb: The same six points reduced two ways: by spread, then by class separation.

steps.title: Six points, two features, two classes
steps.text: Reducing dimensions means going from 2 inputs to 1 while keeping what matters. Red and Blue points differ, but which feature shows that?

steps.title: Measure the spread of each feature
steps.text: x1 runs 1 to 9, with a variance of 64 / 6 = 10.67. x2 only runs 1 to 3, with a variance of 1.

steps.title: PCA (unsupervised): keep the axis with the most variance
steps.text: PCA ignores the class labels and picks the direction where the data is most spread out. Here that is x1. Reduce to that single axis and look at the classes.

steps.title: PCA's result: the classes are mixed
steps.text: On the PC1 axis both Red and Blue sit at 1, 5 and 9, so one dimension no longer tells the classes apart. A lot of spread is not the same as a useful split between classes.

steps.title: LDA (supervised): keep the axis that separates the classes
steps.text: LDA uses the labels and looks for the direction that pulls the classes apart. Here that is x2: every Red is at 1 and every Blue at 3.

steps.title: Compare the two
steps.text: Dropping the other axis (LD2, which is x1) loses nothing for telling the classes apart. These numbers were chosen to make the contrast clear; real data is rarely this tidy.

walkthroughs.title: One-hot encoding
walkthroughs.blurb: Why numbering categories misleads a model and what one-hot does instead.

steps.title: Text a model cannot use
steps.text: scikit-learn needs numbers. The colour column holds words, so it has to be converted.

steps.title: Numbering the categories adds a fake order
steps.text: red = 0, green = 1, blue = 2 looks easy, but it tells the model that blue > green > red, and that green is between the other two. No such order exists.

steps.title: One-hot: one binary column per category
steps.text: Make a column for each colour. Each row has a 1 in the column of its own colour and 0 elsewhere, so no category is bigger than another. In pandas: pd.get_dummies(df['colour']).

steps.title: The cost: more columns
steps.text: 3 categories became 3 columns, and 50 categories would become 50. That growth is why the guide also lists compact styles that write the category number in binary.

walkthroughs.title: Scaling: min-max and standardization
walkthroughs.blurb: The same column scaled both ways, with every calculation shown.

steps.title: A column on its own scale
steps.text: A column of ages: 20, 30, 45, 50, 70. Another column might run 1 to 5, or 0 to 100000. Distance-based methods such as kNN would let the big-valued column dominate, so columns are scaled to comparable ranges.

steps.title: Min-max: find the smallest and largest
steps.text: min = 20, max = 70, so max - min = 50.

steps.title: Min-max: apply the formula to every value
steps.text: (30 - 20) / 50 = 0.2, (45 - 20) / 50 = 0.5, and so on. The smallest value always becomes 0 and the largest 1.

steps.title: Standardization: find the mean
steps.text: (20 + 30 + 45 + 50 + 70) / 5 = 215 / 5 = 43. Subtract it from every value.

steps.title: Standardization: find the standard deviation
steps.text: Average the squares: (529 + 169 + 4 + 49 + 729) / 5 = 1480 / 5 = 296, and the square root is about 17.20. (This is the version scikit-learn's StandardScaler uses; dividing by 4 instead of 5 gives a slightly larger value.)

steps.title: Standardization: apply the formula
steps.text: (20 - 43) / 17.20 = -1.34. The new column has mean 0 and standard deviation 1; values below the mean are negative.

steps.title: Which one to use
steps.text: Min-max gives 0 to 1 and suits data whose distribution is unknown or not bell-shaped, and kNN or neural nets. Standardization gives mean 0 and standard deviation 1 and suits algorithms that assume normally distributed data.

walkthroughs.title: Regularization: L1 versus L2
walkthroughs.blurb: How a penalty on weights narrows the gap between training and test scores.

steps.title: The symptom: a big gap between training and test
steps.text: A model scores 99% on the training data but 72% on the test data. It has memorized noise and outliers in the training rows, which is overfitting.

steps.title: Look at its weights
steps.text: To chase every wiggle in the training data the model uses large weights (coefficients). Features a and b have big values, and c and d are tiny but still counted.

steps.title: Add a penalty on large weights
steps.text: Regularization adds a cost for big weights to the error the model is trying to minimize, so it only keeps a large weight if that weight really helps. The penalty's strength is a hyperparameter that you choose.

steps.title: L2 (Ridge): shrink every weight
steps.text: All the weights get smaller and the outlier-driven swings are smoothed out, but none reaches zero. Most or all features stay in the model.

steps.title: L1 (LASSO): shrink and zero out
steps.text: L1 can push weights to exactly zero. c and d drop out of the model, so LASSO also acts as embedded feature selection.

steps.title: The result: a smaller gap
steps.text: The penalized model fits the training data a little less, but it does much better on the test data. (Example numbers.) More data, feature selection or a larger k for kNN can also help with overfitting.
